summary: Provides an applicability statement for the VPN solution described in RFC 4364 and related documents. It helps readers judge where that approach fits. The document is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo explains when a provider-run private network over MPLS is the right choice. It is right when a customer wants the provider to run the network between its sites, and wrong when the customer wants to keep that control or to build the network over the public Internet.

questions: what is a bgp mpls vpn
when should i use a bgp mpls vpn
subtitle: When a provider-run private network over MPLS is the right answer, and when it is not.

tldr.problem: An enterprise that wants its sites connected privately has to choose who runs the network between them, and the choice of mechanism determines what it can control.
tldr.mechanism: The memo describes how a provider builds each VPN as a separate routing table on its edge routers, with route targets deciding which tables exchange routes, and BGP carrying those routes across the provider's MPLS backbone.
tldr.outcome: The memo gives a checklist of what fits and what does not, and notes that the service protects routing and isolation between customers but says nothing about encrypting the customer data itself.

today: RFC 4365 is an Informational memo published in February 2006, and the metadata records no obsoleting or updating RFC. It is an applicability statement for the service defined in RFC 4364, so it says which situations the design suits and which they do not.

sections.title: Who This Service Is For
sections.content:
This document is an applicability statement for the virtual private network solution described in RFC 4364 and the other documents in its reference list. They are called BGP/MPLS IP VPNs because BGP distributes the routes and Multiprotocol Label Switching marks the packets that need to follow particular routes.

A VPN service is provided by a service provider to a customer, sometimes called an enterprise. The arrangement suits a customer who uses the VPN only to carry IP packets, who does not want to run a routed backbone and would rather outsource inter-site routing to the provider, and who wants the provider's backbone and its routing to be completely transparent. If the customer has a routed infrastructure at its own sites, it does not want its site routing to know anything about the provider's backbone, either its native structure or an overlay of tunnels. On the provider side, the arrangement suits a provider with an IP backbone and MPLS-enabled edge routers, who wants to offer that service and does not want to maintain a separate overlay of tunnels for each customer.

The basic principle is to model each VPN as a self-contained internet: each site makes one or more access connections to the provider, sends the provider its routing information, and relies on the provider to distribute that information to the other sites in the same VPN. It differs from internet service because the provider strictly controls the distribution of routing information, so that routes from inside a VPN are not sent outside it unless the customer explicitly authorizes that. Even within the VPN, the distribution of routes may be controlled to meet a customer policy.

Two cases are explicitly out of scope. Customers who want to connect their sites over the public Internet, buying connectivity for each site from whichever provider is cheapest, need an overlay of secure tunnels instead. And customers who want complete control over the routing in their own backbone will not want a managed routing service, since that hides the backbone's details; they may prefer a virtual router service, where the tunnels appear as links to the customer's own routing algorithm. Remote offices and telecommuters that must reach the VPN over the public Internet are a different matter: their traffic can be tunnelled to a provider edge router, which then treats it as if it had arrived on a local access link, though quality of service and service level agreement issues must then be considered.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo explains when a provider-run private network over MPLS is the right choice. It is right when a customer wants the provider to run the network between its sites, and wrong when the customer wants to keep that control or to build the network over the public Internet.

sections.title: How The Provider Builds A VPN
sections.content:
When a VPN attaches to a provider edge router, the provider must configure that router with a VPN Routing and Forwarding table, a routing table specific to that VPN, also called a VPN Forwarding Instance. Each interface or sub-interface at that router that attaches to a site in the VPN must be configured so that it is associated with the table. The table is filled automatically with routes from locally attached customer edge routers, using whatever routing protocol runs on the access links, and with routes from other tables distributed by BGP. Static configuration is optional.

Each provider edge router must run BGP and be pre-configured with the identities of a small set of BGP route reflectors, with which it peers using IBGP. In lieu of route reflectors one could configure every edge router with the identity of all the others and build a full mesh, which may be adequate for small networks but does not scale, so route reflectors are needed for scalability.

Each table must be configured with three parameters. The Route Distinguisher is a globally unique 8-byte value; each table may have its own, or a single value may serve a whole VPN. When BGP carries VPN routing information across the backbone, this value is prepended to the VPN's IPv4 prefixes, creating the VPN-IPv4 address family, so that two VPNs with overlapping address space still have distinct address spaces. The Export Route Targets are one or more globally unique 8-byte values that BGP carries, in the Extended Communities Route Target attribute, along with the routes exported from the table. The Import Route Targets select which routes are imported from other tables into this one.

In the simplest and most common cases the export target, import target and distinguisher can be identical, and all the tables in one VPN will distribute routes to each other, which is the typical intranet. Setting them differently allows fine-grained control over which routes go where, which can be used to build extranets or enforce customer policy. In complicated cases particular export targets can be assigned to particular routes using router management mechanisms. One advantage of not requiring the distinguisher to match a target is that the distinguisher value can be determined automatically for each table, while target values must always be configured.
sections.plainLanguage: Each VPN gets its own routing table on the provider's edge routers. Two eight-byte numbers decide who talks to whom: a route distinguisher keeps two VPNs with the same addresses apart, and route targets decide which tables exchange routes.

sections.title: Topologies, Traffic Types And Isolation
sections.content:
The scheme is optimized for full inter-site connectivity, which is what the simplest configurations give. The provider has full control, through route targets, over the distribution of routing information between tables, so it can also offer hub-and-spoke or partial mesh connectivity. Strictly speaking the scheme does not create a topology, because it creates no layer 2 connections between sites, but it does allow control over the IP connectivity between them, and that control can be arbitrary: the routes from site A can be distributed to one set of remote sites while other routes from site A go to a different set, and it is possible to require that data from site A to site B travels through a third site C, down to the granularity of a single route.

Unicast IP traffic is fully supported and customer packets pass through transparently. Multicast is optionally supported, if the provider offers the optional mechanisms for it, though there are scaling implications. Non-IP traffic is not supported: if it is needed, the provider must also offer a layer 2 tunnelling service, or the customer must use IP tunnelling.

Customer routers at different sites do not normally become routing peers, but a customer may allow it over a link that is not part of the VPN service, and such peering relationships are known as IGP backdoors. So that the customer's routing works correctly when backdoors are present, each VPN route distributed by the provider is distributed with a corresponding routing metric, so the customer's IGP can compare backdoor routes properly with routes that use the provider's backbone.

The route target mechanism keeps routing information inside its VPN. VPN routes are treated by BGP as a different address family from ordinary internet routes, so they are not leaked to the internet unless the table is explicitly configured to allow it, and this is not the default. The way a VPN is divided into sites, and the topology of any particular site, is hidden from the internet and from other VPNs. Internet routes do not get imported unless the table is configured to ask for them. Proper configuration is essential: each access link must be associated with the right table, and each table must have the right set of route targets. Where two VPNs attach to the same edge router, there is strict separation of both forwarding and routing information. Data travelling between two customer sites is encapsulated while in transit, and the encapsulation carries enough information to send the packet to the right edge router and, with the table there, to the right customer router.
sections.plainLanguage: The provider decides which sites can reach which by setting route targets, so a full mesh, a hub and spoke, or an extranet are all possible. Customer packets are wrapped up for the trip and unwrapped at the far end. Only IP traffic is carried.

sections.title: Addressing And Access
sections.content:
Overlapping customer addresses are supported, and there is no requirement that they conform to the private address ranges of RFC 1918, nor that customer addresses be distinct from the provider's own. Any set of addresses can be supported regardless of how they are assigned, how well they aggregate, or whether they are public or private, though the set of addresses reachable from a given site must be unique. Address translation on packets leaving or entering a VPN is possible and is transparent to the scheme. Nothing in the architecture prevents it from being extended to IPv6, provided the routing between customer and provider edge routers supports IPv6 and the provider-to-provider BGP supports the labelled IPv6 address family, which had not been specified but is said to follow from the labelled IPv4 one. The provider's backbone IGP does not itself need to be IPv6 capable to carry customer IPv6 networks. Layer 2 addresses and identifiers are never carried across the backbone.

The architecture does not restrict the physical or link layer at all. Temporary access over PPP is possible using standard PPP-based authentication: the provider's authentication server authenticates the user and returns a VPN identifier, the edge router puts the user in the right table, and the customer's own authentication server then gets a chance to authenticate the session too. The user is disconnected if either step fails. IPsec access to a table is also possible, with the security association between the end user and the provider. A customer edge router can be homed to two or more provider edge routers, whether or not they are on the same provider network. There is no explicit support for mobility beyond this.
sections.plainLanguage: Customers can use whatever addresses they like, even the same ones as another customer, and even the provider's own. Dial-up and IPsec users can reach a VPN from the public Internet, and a site can connect to more than one provider edge router.

sections.title: Scalability And Quality Of Service
sections.content:
There is no upper limit on the number of VPNs per provider network, because no single box has to know about all of them. Knowledge of a particular VPN is confined to the edge routers attached to its sites and to the route reflectors that receive routing data from those edge routers; other systems keep no state for it at all. Over an MPLS backbone, the backbone IGP must carry a host route for every label switched path egress node in the routing domain, and every provider edge router is one, so the sum of the edge routers and border routers in a domain is limited by the number of routes the domain's IGP can carry, which does not seem to create a practical problem. There is no upper limit on the number of site interfaces per VPN, since state for an interface is kept only at the edge router it attaches to.

The major constraint is the number of routes a given edge router can support, which depends on the set of VPNs attached to it, the number of routes in each, and the number of ordinary internet routes it must also handle. If the limits are reached, the provider may have to replace the router with a larger one or reorganize how access links lead from customer routers to edge routers, concentrating the links from sites in the same VPN. Rehoming a site may not involve rewiring at all, and can also be done virtually with a layer 2 tunnel from the old edge router to the new one. One important point is that a provider may run any number of independent BGP systems carrying VPN routes, unlike the internet where one BGP system must carry every route, because all internet addresses must be reachable from each other but a VPN address only has to be reachable from addresses in the same VPN.

Quality of service and service level agreements are covered in a separate section. The provider's backbone has to support the quality of service the customer has bought, and the memo discusses the mechanisms for this and the effect of the VPN scheme on them.
sections.plainLanguage: There is no limit on how many VPNs a provider can run, because no single router holds them all. The real limit is how many routes one edge router can carry, and the provider has to plan for that.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
No particular means of protecting user data is specified for this service. Optional procedures may be used to authenticate or encrypt user data as it travels from the ingress edge router to the egress one, but the data is exposed at those two routers and on the access links. The customer can provide his own data security by using IPsec tunnels that terminate inside the customer sites, and such tunnels are transparent to the VPN scheme, as is end-to-end transport mode IPsec, as long as a cleartext IP header passes from the customer router to the provider's. When data must cross the internet to reach an ingress router, IPsec tunnels between the end user and that router can be used, and the router must then associate each tunnel with the right table.

The provider is responsible for keeping illegitimate traffic out of a VPN. Because VPN traffic is always encapsulated on the backbone, this is a matter of making sure the edge routers encapsulate and decapsulate correctly and that encapsulations have not been spoofed. The provider's own routers must be secure against break-ins, neither provider nor edge routers should form routing adjacencies with each other without some security such as authentication in the IGP or physical security, and the access link should be secured in some manner. Label distribution sessions and BGP sessions between provider routers should be authenticated, using the TCP MD5 option or IPsec. If the service runs over MPLS, the provider should not accept MPLS packets from external interfaces unless the top label was legitimately distributed to the system the packet came from, and if it uses IP encapsulation or accepts encapsulated packets from other providers it should filter at its borders so it does not accept packets addressed to its own edge routers without an appropriate trust relationship.

One further risk is on the access link: when a dynamic routing protocol runs between the customer router and the edge router, routing instability in the customer's network can affect the edge router, for example an unusually large number of routing updates placing a large processing load on it, which could be used as a denial of service attack. The memo suggests partitioning resources in the edge router so that no one VPN can use too much, applying rate limits to the routing traffic, or shutting the customer-to-provider interface down when the problem is detected.
sections.plainLanguage: The service keeps customers' routes apart but does not encrypt customer traffic. The provider has to keep its own routers safe and make sure nobody can inject packets that look like they came from a real provider router.

viz.caption: WHERE THE SERVICE FITS AND WHERE IT DOES NOT (RFC 4365 SECTION 1)

cells: A customer that only carries IP and wants the provider to run its backbone
Yes, this is the intended case
A customer that wants to connect its sites over the public Internet
No; use an overlay of secure tunnels instead
A customer that wants full control of its own backbone routing
No; consider a virtual router service
Remote users who must reach the VPN over the public Internet
Yes, by tunnelling the traffic to a provider edge router
A VPN spread over hundreds of service providers
Not the design centre; a few cooperating providers is the intended case

viz.caption: WHAT THE PROVIDER CONFIGURES FOR EACH VPN (RFC 4365 SECTION 2)

items.title: VRF
items.text: A routing table on the provider edge router, specific to one VPN. Each access link is configured to be associated with it.

items.title: Route Distinguisher
items.text: A globally unique 8-byte value prepended to the VPN's address prefixes, so two VPNs with overlapping address space stay distinct.

items.title: Export Route Target
items.text: A globally unique 8-byte value carried with the routes leaving the table, telling other tables which of them should receive them.

items.title: Import Route Target
items.text: A globally unique 8-byte value that selects which routes from other tables are imported into this one.

items.title: Route Reflectors
items.text: Each edge router runs BGP and peers with a small set of route reflectors rather than a full mesh with every other edge router.

viz.caption: A PACKET CROSSING THE BACKBONE, ILLUSTRATIVE (RFC 4365)

messages.label: Site routes
messages.note: The customer's router sends its routing information to the provider edge router.

messages.label: Labelled packet
messages.note: The packet is encapsulated with a label that tells the backbone which VPN it belongs to and where to send it.

messages.label: Delivered packet
messages.note: The far provider edge router decapsulates the packet and forwards it into the right VPN routing table.
